points.description: Proves that AT_A, BT_B, CT_C are concurrent at a point P (any valid method). Typical: AT_A is isogonal to the cevian AN_A, where N_A is the tangency point of the A-excircle with BC, so the lines concur at the isogonal conjugate of the Nagel point. Other proofs are fine, such as trig Ceva with the mixtilinear tangency ratio, or the exsimilicenter and Ceva method. The key facts used must be proved or be well-known lemmas that are clearly stated. A bare assertion of concurrency earns no more than half.

levels.says: States concurrency, or the isogonal/Nagel lemma, with little or no justification, or the proof has a significant gap.

points.description: Shows P has equal power with respect to ω and each of the circles (ADT_A), (BET_B), (CFT_C). Reason: P lies on chord AT_A of ω and on the secant AT_A of circle ADT_A, so the power is PA·PT_A for both, and likewise for B and C. So P lies on the radical axis of every pair of the three circles. The common value is the power of P in ω, which is negative because P is inside ω.

Finds a second point Q, or an equivalent second condition, with equal power with respect to all three circles. Q must be genuinely different from P and must be justified for all three circles by the same argument. Examples are a point on line AD, a computation via inversion at A with power bc composed with reflection in the bisector, which sends D to the arc midpoint M_A, ω to BC and T_A to N_A, or a coaxiality argument. An answer that only asserts the circles are coaxial, with no proof, earns nothing here.

levels.says: Proposes a plausible second point or axis and proves the equal-power property for only one circle, or with a major gap.

points.description: Concludes the argument. The three circles share the radical axis PQ, so they form a coaxial family. They meet the axis in two points X and Y, and the intersection is real because P is inside all three circles (negative power). X and Y are distinct and common to all three circles. The student must address why the circles are distinct and intersect in two points, not just a tangency or no intersection.

rubric.notes: Full marks need the concurrency at P, equal power of P, a proof of a second equal-power point (coaxiality), and the conclusion that two common points exist. The grading guidelines give about 1/7 for showing the concurrency alone, so a solution with only P1 should score about 1 to 2. Award marks for any valid alternative method, and do not award P3 or P4 for unsupported claims that the circles are coaxial.
rubric.answer_key: Plan: (1) Let N_A be the A-excircle touch point on BC. It is known that AT_A and AN_A are isogonal in angle A. By Ceva, AN_A, BN_B, CN_C concur at the Nagel point. So AT_A, BT_B, CT_C concur at its isogonal conjugate P, which is inside the triangle and so inside ω. (2) P lies on the line AT_A, a common secant of ω and of circle (ADT_A). So pow(P, ADT_A) = PA·PT_A = pow(P, ω), and similarly for B and C. All three circles have the same power -k, with k>0, at P. (3) A second point Q with equal power for the three circles is needed. For example, apply the inversion at A with power bc followed by reflection in AI. It swaps B and C, sends ω to line BC and T_A to N_A, and sends D to the arc midpoint M_A of BC on ω, since AD·AM_A=bc. The circle (ADT_A) goes to line N_A M_A. A common radical axis follows if the three lines or their images give a second common equal-power point. The marker should accept any rigorous proof that the three circles are coaxial with axis PQ. (4) Since P is inside all three circles, the common radical axis through P meets each circle at two points. These two points X and Y are common to all three circles. Final: the circles of ADT_A, BET_B and CFT_C pass through the same two points X and Y.

selftest_notes: The model answer scored only 2.8 of 7.
